Calculate test coverage for sets of files

Source: R/file_coverage.R
file_coverage.Rd

The files in source_files are first sourced into a new environment to define functions to be checked. Then they are instrumented to track coverage and the files in test_files are run with runner.

Usage

file_coverage(
  source_files,
  test_files,
  line_exclusions = NULL,
  function_exclusions = NULL,
  parent_env = parent.frame(),
  runner = source_test_file
)

Arguments

source_files

Character vector of source files with function definitions to measure coverage. Can also include compiled files from a package's src/ directory; see the compiled code section.

test_files

Character vector of test files with code to test the functions

line_exclusions

a named list of files with the lines to exclude from each file.

function_exclusions

a vector of regular expressions matching function names to exclude. Example print\\\. to match print methods.

parent_env

The parent environment to use when sourcing the files. If source_files includes compiled files, the default is the namespace of their package.

runner

A function used to run each test file, called as runner(file, env = env), where env is the environment the source_files were sourced into. The default sources the file into env with sys.source(). Use runner = testthat::test_file to run testthat tests with testthat's test runner; see the testthat tests section.

Value

A coverage object.

Parallel code

Code run in processes forked by parallel::mclapply(), parallel::mcparallel() and related functions (not available on Windows) is included in the coverage. While the code runs, parallel:::mcfork and parallel:::mcexit are patched so that the forked processes save their counts when they exit. To turn this off, set the option covr.fix_parallel_mcexit or the environment variable COVR_FIX_PARALLEL_MCEXIT to FALSE.

testthat tests

By default the test files are run with sys.source(), not with testthat's test runner, so features that need the runner don't work. In particular, testthat::expect_snapshot() is skipped ("Can't compare snapshot to reference when testing interactively").

To use these features, run the test files with testthat::test_file():

file_coverage(
  "R/my_functions.R",
  "tests/test-my_functions.R",
  runner = testthat::test_file
)

The tests then run in a child of the environment the source files were sourced into, and snapshots are saved in a _snaps directory next to the test file. expect_snapshot() also needs testthat's 3rd edition (e.g. testthat::local_edition(3) in the tests), and is skipped unless the NOT_CRAN environment variable is "true".

For more control, source the files yourself and use with_coverage().

Files from a package

To make the package's other functions available, load the package (e.g. with pkgload::load_all()) and use parent_env = asNamespace("pkg"). Calls from other package files use the namespace's untraced functions, so don't count. devtools::test_coverage_active_file() measures the coverage of one file of a package without this limitation.

Compiled code

environment_coverage() and with_coverage() include the compiled code in the coverage of the namespace of a package loaded with pkgload::load_all() (e.g. by devtools::load_all()), so devtools::test_coverage_active_file() also works for files in src/. With compiled files in source_files, file_coverage() loads their package with pkgload::load_all() and reports the coverage of those files, without needing devtools:

file_coverage("src/foo.c", "tests/testthat/test-foo.R")
file_coverage("src/rust/src/lib.rs", "tests/testthat/test-foo.R")

The compiled code is measured in the current session, which is much faster than package_coverage(): C, C++, Fortran and Objective-C code with gcov, and Rust code (e.g. of packages using extendr or savvy) with LLVM's source-based coverage, which needs the llvm tools described in package_coverage(). An instrumented copy of the package is built in the session's temporary directory, leaving the package's own build untouched, and later runs only recompile the files that changed, with cargo's incremental build in the copy's own target directory for Rust code. While the code runs, the namespace's native routines use the instrumented DLL instead of the package's own. Routines that were looked up some other way, e.g. stored by .onLoad() or found by other packages with R_GetCCallable(), keep using the package's DLL, so their code isn't counted. Set options(covr.gcov = "") to leave out C, C++, Fortran and Objective-C code, and options(covr.llvm_cov = "") to leave out Rust code.

Examples

# Save code and tests to temporary files
source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
test_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".R")
cat("add <- function(x, y) { x + y }", file = source_file)
cat("add(1, 2) == 3", file = test_file)

# Use file_coverage() to calculate test coverage
file_coverage(source_files = source_file, test_files = test_file)
#> Coverage: 100.00%
#> /tmp/RtmpOeHbfo/file196729fa4b0a.R: 100.00%
